teaching.text: Blood return through a 21G needle is slower than through an 18G needle.

Advance the micropuncture wire only under fluoroscopy: its angled tip can enter small branches. One series saw retroperitoneal bleeding in 0.7% with micropuncture versus 0.18% with a standard needle, attributed to that tip.

target.text: Anterior wall of the common femoral artery below the femoral head centerline and relatively high within the lower inner quadrant of the femoral head (the artery is almost always medial); above the bifurcation and below the inferior epigastric artery

facts.text: Punctures above the inferior epigastric artery carry odds ratios for retroperitoneal hemorrhage as high as 17:1.
High punctures correlate with retroperitoneal hemorrhage; low punctures with pseudoaneurysm, hematoma and arteriovenous fistula.
The inguinal crease is the single most common landmark (40% of operators) but does not reliably overlie the femoral head.
Run a femoral angiogram through the sheath before anticoagulation to confirm the arteriotomy level.

frequencies.label: Bifurcation above the bottom of the femoral head (type 2)
Bifurcation below the middle third of the femoral head
Puncture over the middle third of the femoral head lies at or above the inferior epigastric artery
frequencies.note: More common in obese patients. This is the inferior epigastric artery's position, not the bifurcation's.

sequence.text: Micropuncture: puncture over the femoral head, expect slower return through the 21G needle, advance the 0.018 in wire under fluoroscopy, place the 4F introducer, run a sheath angiogram in an oblique projection, exchange to a 0.035 in wire, upsize.
